stimulus.text: "Each side had advantages. But neither section understood the other. If the South had known that secession must result in war and that the foe would be a united North, it is doubtful if she would have proceeded to the last extremity. … But now the North confronted five and a half million earnest and brave people, supported by three and a half million servants, who grew the food and took care of the women and children at home while the men fought in the field." —James Ford Rhodes, History of the Civil War, 1917 (abridged)

parts: A. Briefly explain Rhodes's perspective on Northern and Southern attitudes at the start of the war.
B. Briefly explain ONE historical event or development that supports Rhodes's argument.
C. Briefly explain ONE historical event or development that illustrates an unwillingness on one side to compromise before the war.
exemplar: Rhodes argues that both sides misread each other: the South did not expect the North to unite and fight for the Union, and the North did not expect the South to unite behind secession.
The First Battle of Bull Run (1861) supports Rhodes: Northerners expected a quick, easy victory, but the Confederate stand showed the South was united and determined to fight.
The failure of the Crittenden Compromise in early 1861 shows unwillingness to compromise: Republicans rejected any deal extending slavery's protection, and seceding states refused to return.
Wilson calls for a permanent international organization - a League of Nations - that would collectively guarantee the independence and borders of all states, large and small.
The unprecedented slaughter of World War I, which killed millions and shattered European empires, convinced Wilson that only a new system of collective security could prevent future wars.
The Senate's rejection of the Treaty of Versailles (1919-1920), led by Henry Cabot Lodge over the League covenant and Article X, kept the United States out of the League Wilson had proposed.
parts: A. Briefly describe Wilson's proposal in the excerpt.
B. Briefly explain ONE reason Wilson believed a new international system was necessary.
C. Briefly explain ONE reason the United States did not join the organization Wilson proposed.

stimulus.attribution: Woodrow Wilson, Fourteen Points (Point XIV), address to Congress, January 8, 1918.
stimulus.text: A general association of nations must be formed under specific covenants for the purpose of affording mutual guarantees of political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike.

The timeline shows: 1803 — Louisiana Purchase, as Napoleon abandons his American empire; 1807 — Embargo Act halts American trade with Britain and France; 1812–1815 — War of 1812 with Britain; 1814 — Hartford Convention of anti-war Federalists; 1815 — Battle of New Orleans makes Andrew Jackson a hero.

parts: A. Briefly explain ONE example of how foreign wars influenced American policy in the period 1801–1815.
B. Briefly explain a SECOND example of that influence in the same period.
C. Briefly explain ONE consequence of the War of 1812.
exemplar: Napoleon's failure to crush the Haitian slave rebellion, combined with looming war against Britain, convinced him to sell Louisiana in 1803 — doubling the United States at a stroke.

Jefferson's 1807 Embargo Act, a response to British and French seizures of American ships during the Napoleonic Wars, devastated American commerce and showed how European wars dictated American policy.
The War of 1812 fostered American nationalism and economic independence: the war spurred domestic manufacturing, discredited the Federalists after Hartford, and ushered in the 'Era of Good Feelings.'
